sheets.lifecycle: Runs once per pull request when the CI job executes and ends when the process exits. It stops applying when the job is removed from the pipeline; there is no resident configuration to go stale.
sheets.failure_mode: The configuration half fails closed, the reproducibility half does not: identical flags make the loaded config identical, but the model's output is not byte-for-byte deterministic, and the model version the job resolves to can change under it. So the promise you can actually keep is a reproducible environment, not a reproducible string. Also be aware --bare narrows Claude to Bash, file read and file edit tools, so a prompt that assumed an MCP tool silently loses it.
sheets.version_caveat: --bare sets CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE and is the fastest way to strip discovery; do not substitute --safe-mode (v2.1.169 and later), which disables customizations but still applies managed settings policy including policy-configured hooks, so it is not equivalent for isolation. Whether managed policy also survives --bare is not spelled out in the documentation I have, so pin the runner image if that matters. --strict-mcp-config does not filter servers passed inline via --agents or the SDK agents option, since those count as explicit caller input.

sheets.primary: A headless Agent SDK / CLI invocation from the CI job: claude -p with the review instructions passed in the prompt and configuration pinned on the command line, using --strict-mcp-config with no --mcp-config so zero MCP servers load, plus --setting-sources (or --bare) to suppress discovery of user hooks, skills, plugins, auto memory and CLAUDE.md. Everything the run depends on is an argument, not something found on the machine.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A project skill checked into the repo holding the review instructions. It loses because a skill is still discovered configuration: it is resolved alongside whatever user-scope hooks, plugins and .mcp.json entries happen to exist on the runner, which is exactly the leakage the requirement forbids.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The isolation is a startup-time property of the CLI flags, evaluated before any model turn, so no prompt or repo content can re-enable a server or a user hook mid-run.
sheets.context_boundary: One fresh, single-turn context window per CI invocation, holding only the system prompt, the explicit instructions and the piped diff. Nothing persists between pull requests, and no developer session state crosses in.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the CI step launches the process with the diff on stdin and ends when the process prints its response and exits. There is no resumption; the next pull request gets a brand-new process.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open in two specific ways worth designing around. First, the isolation flags are not total: --strict-mcp-config does not filter servers passed inline via --agents or the SDK agents option, and managed-settings policy still applies to every run. Second, and more fundamentally, these flags make the configuration reproducible, not the output: nothing in the documented flag set guarantees byte-identical model text across runs, so treat exact-output reproducibility as an unverified assumption and pin whatever you can (model id, temperature-equivalent settings, prompt) at the caller.
sheets.version_caveat: --safe-mode, the stronger customization-disabling switch, needs v2.1.169 or later; if the org wants to guarantee nobody re-enables sideloaded config, disableSideloadFlags (managed settings only, rejecting --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents and --mcp-config at startup) requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later, and it does not block .mcp.json or claude mcp add.

scenarios.scenario: Compliance needs an accurate record of every shell command the agent actually executed on developer machines, captured automatically with the full command line, rather than relying on the model to self-report what it ran.

key.primary: PostToolUse hook with a Bash matcher whose command appends the executed command and its result from the hook's stdin JSON to an audit log
key.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher that logs each command
key.rejection_reason: PreToolUse fires before permission evaluation and before the call runs, so it records attempts that a deny rule, a hook, or the user subsequently blocked; the audit trail would contain commands that never executed. PostToolUse fires only after the tool call succeeds, and logging operations is one of its documented use cases.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the hook is a shell process that receives the executed command and its result as JSON on stdin); the audit trail flows outward to a log file on disk, and nothing returns to Claude's context from a logging hook that exits 0 quietly
key.lifecycle: PostToolUse event fires after each successful Bash tool call, receiving tool input and result on stdin
key.failure_mode: It captures successes only: commands that error need a companion PostToolUseFailure hook, and the log lives on each developer's machine unless the hook itself ships entries to central storage.

sheets.primary: A hook pair on the Bash tool deployed through managed settings: a PreToolUse hook with matcher "Bash" that appends .tool_input.command plus session_id, cwd and a timestamp to the audit sink, and PostToolUse plus PostToolUseFailure hooks that record the outcome. Use type "http" to POST to a central audit service rather than a local file when the record must survive the developer's machine.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Instructing the model to log what it ran, via CLAUDE.md or a skill. That is self-report, exactly what the requirement rules out, and it is least reliable in the cases compliance cares about.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code invokes the hook with the exact tool_input it is about to execute, independent of anything the model says it did.
sheets.context_boundary: The hooks run outside the model's context window, receive the tool call JSON on stdin, and write to a file or HTTP endpoint without returning anything to the conversation. The model is never told the audit exists and cannot shape or suppress the record.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every Bash tool call in every session on machines carrying the managed policy, including calls made inside subagents (the input carries agent_id and agent_type). It stops only if the managed hook entry is removed, since disableAllHooks in user, project or local settings cannot disable a managed hook.
sheets.failure_mode: PreToolUse records intent, so a command later blocked by a deny rule still appears in the log, and PostToolUse alone would miss failed commands, which is why PostToolUseFailure is paired with it. Coverage is per tool call, not per process: whatever a shell script or make target spawns internally is invisible, the separate PowerShell tool needs its own matcher, and a log file on the audited developer's own disk is writable by them, so ship it off-box.
sheets.version_caveat: Set allowManagedHooksOnly to true in managed settings so no user, project or unvetted plugin hook can run alongside; that key is managed-settings-only, and hooks from plugins force-enabled in managed enabledPlugins remain exempt. For HTTP delivery, allowedHttpHookUrls and httpHookAllowedEnvVars constrain the destination and the interpolated secrets, and non-2xx responses, connection failures and timeouts on an HTTP hook are non-blocking errors, so records can be lost silently.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool that appends the full command string, timestamp, session id, user and working directory to an append-only audit sink, paired with a PostToolUse hook on the same tool that records the outcome so the record distinguishes attempted from executed. It is deployed through managed settings so developers do not opt out, and it writes to a location the developer cannot rewrite (a syslog/SIEM forwarder rather than a file in their home directory).
sheets.rejected_alternative: Reconstructing the record from session transcripts after the fact, rejected because transcripts are local, user-modifiable, and describe what was said as much as what ran.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook receives the actual tool input the harness is about to execute, so the record does not depend on the model reporting honestly.
sheets.context_boundary: Logging happens in a separate process on the tool payload, and it returns nothing to the agent, so the audit trail costs no context and the model has no view of what was recorded.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every Bash tool invocation while the managed configuration is in force. It stops covering anything the moment work moves to a machine or an install that does not load the policy.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open by design, since a logging hook that errors should not stop the developer, which means a broken forwarder produces silence rather than an alarm; the sink therefore needs its own heartbeat. Coverage is also narrower than the compliance ask sounds: it captures the command the agent submitted, not what a spawned shell, a build script, an interactive process, or an MCP server subsequently executed, and a locally written log file is tamperable.
sheets.version_caveat: This depends on the hook payload exposing the command verbatim under a stable field for the Bash tool, and on managed settings being able to define hooks that project and user settings cannot override. I cannot confirm either the field name or the override precedence for hooks from model knowledge alone. There may also be a first-party telemetry/OTel export that satisfies this more cleanly, possibly plan-gated, which should be checked before building custom logging.

sheets.primary: A pair of logging hooks shipped in managed settings: PostToolUse with matcher Bash and PostToolUseFailure with matcher Bash, each appending tool_input.command together with session_id and a timestamp to an append-only audit file or an HTTP audit endpoint.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse logging hook. It loses for this need because it records what the agent attempted, including calls that a deny rule or a human later refused, so it documents intent rather than execution, which is the opposite of what compliance asked for.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs the hook at the lifecycle point with the real tool input, so the record is captured mechanically rather than narrated by the model.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs out of process once per Bash tool call with the full hook JSON on stdin, so the audit record is written outside the conversation entirely. Nothing needs to cross back into the context window, and the model is neither asked to confirm nor able to edit what was written.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires after each Bash tool call resolves, PostToolUse on success and PostToolUseFailure on error, in every session on machines that load the hook. It stops applying if the settings source is removed, and it never fires in a session that uses no Bash tool.
sheets.failure_mode: Non-blocking by design, so it fails open: the tool has already run by the time the hook fires, and a failed log write stops nothing. The real risk is coverage rather than blocking. One Bash call that runs a script yields one log line, not the commands inside the script, and PostToolUse on its own misses commands that errored, which is why PostToolUseFailure is paired with it.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on the events themselves. To make the record non-removable by developers, the managed-settings-only allowManagedHooksOnly flag is required, so that user hooks, project hooks and unvetted plugin hooks do not load and nobody can substitute a neutered logger.

sheets.primary: A command hook on the Bash tool events, deployed through managed settings: a PreToolUse handler with matcher "Bash" that appends tool_input.command with a timestamp and session_id to an append-only audit log, paired with a PostToolUse handler on the same matcher so the record distinguishes attempted from actually executed. The harness supplies the full command line, so nothing depends on the model describing what it ran.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md or rules instructing the model to log each command it runs, which is self-report by another name: advisory, unverifiable, and silently incomplete the first time the model omits an entry.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs every matching handler when the event fires, so capture does not depend on model cooperation; completeness of the record then depends on the handler being present at the managed tier.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler is a separate process on the developer machine; the tool-call JSON crosses in on stdin and the log line is written locally, with nothing crossing back into the model's context. Shipping the log off-box is a separate transport the hook must perform.
sheets.lifecycle: PreToolUse runs after Claude has formed the tool parameters and before the call is processed, on every Bash invocation for the life of the session; PostToolUse runs after a call completes successfully. Capture ends when the hook entry is removed or hooks are disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: a PreToolUse logging hook exits 0 and never blocks, and a log written before the call means a command later denied by a rule or a sibling hook still appears in the record, which overstates execution unless the PostToolUse side is also captured. The log misses shell activity that never goes through the Bash tool, such as commands a spawned script runs on its own.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate applies to the events themselves. The tamper gate does: allowManagedHooksOnly, which blocks user, project and non-approved plugin hooks so only the IT-shipped logger loads, can only be set in managed settings, and without it a developer can neutralise the audit with disableAllHooks.

scenarios.scenario: We want to shut off the entire aws CLI surface for the agent except one approved read-only invocation, aws s3 ls, which should go through without prompting. Every other aws command must be refused outright.

key.primary: PreToolUse hook on Bash that inspects the command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for aws commands unless they match the approved invocation (returning "allow" for that one)
key.rejected_alternative: permissions.deny Bash(aws *) paired with permissions.allow Bash(aws s3 ls)
key.rejection_reason: Rules evaluate in fixed deny, then ask, then allow order and the first match wins; rule specificity does not change the order. The permissions docs state a broad deny like Bash(aws *) blocks every matching call including ones a narrower allow also matches, so a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions. Exception logic must live in a PreToolUse hook, which the docs recommend for exactly this allow-everything-except pattern, and no deny rule for aws may remain in settings since deny rules override hook allow decisions.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the script runs as a shell process before each Bash tool call reaches execution); on a deny decision the reason crosses into the main conversation and is shown to Claude, while on an allow decision the reason is shown to the user but not Claude and the call simply proceeds
key.lifecycle: PreToolUse event fires before each Bash tool call, ahead of permission rules and any prompt
key.failure_mode: The hook script must handle compound commands itself: a naive check passes 'aws s3 ls && aws iam delete-user', and the protection exists only on machines where the hook is configured.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool, handler filtered with if: "Bash(aws *)", that parses tool_input.command, checks every subcommand, and returns permissionDecision "allow" only for an exact aws s3 ls invocation and "deny" for anything else beginning with aws. The whole allowlist has to live inside the hook, because permission rules alone cannot express deny-with-one-exception.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A permissions.deny rule "Bash(aws *)" paired with a permissions.allow rule for "Bash(aws s3 ls)", which is the obvious construction and does not work: deny is evaluated first and a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions, so the approved command is blocked along with everything else.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness runs the hook and applies its decision before the permission prompt, but the correctness of the allowlist is owned by the handler code you write, so this is harness-enforced with author-owned judgment.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler runs in a separate process with the command string on stdin; the deny reason crosses back into the model's context as the tool outcome, and the allowed command runs with no prompt to the human.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs on every Bash tool call, before the permission prompt, whenever the if filter matches or cannot parse the command, for as long as the hook is configured; it stops applying if hooks are disabled or the entry is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on handler failure: any exit code other than 2 lets the call proceed to the normal permission flow, and under an auto-approving mode that means an unreviewed aws command runs. The other real hole is parsing, since compound commands, command substitution, wrappers and variable indirection must all be handled by your own check, so treat every unrecognised shape as deny.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate is documented in the mirror for the if filter or for the PreToolUse permissionDecision values. The binding constraint is precedence, not version: a hook returning "allow" never overrides a deny or ask rule at any version, so you must not also add a deny rule for aws, or the exception can never be granted.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook with matcher "Bash" that parses the command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for any aws invocation that is not exactly `aws s3 ls`, paired with a permissions.allow rule "Bash(aws s3 ls)" so the one approved call runs without a prompt. The hook supplies the exception logic that permission rules structurally cannot express.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Permission rules alone: deny "Bash(aws *)" with allow "Bash(aws s3 ls)". Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and specificity does not change that order, so the broad deny swallows the narrow allow. The documentation states outright that a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions, so this configuration blocks aws s3 ls too.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness for both halves: Claude Code runs the hook and applies the allow rule. The model never sees the policy, only the refusal reason.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook subprocess receives the full command string on stdin and decides outside the model's context window; only permissionDecisionReason crosses back so Claude learns why the call was refused and can stop retrying. Deliberately keeping any `Bash(aws *)` deny rule out of settings is what lets the allow rule reach the approved call at all.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs before every Bash tool call for the life of the session, in every permission mode including bypassPermissions and dontAsk, since PreToolUse fires before the permission-mode check. It applies until the hook entry is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for what the script recognizes and open for what it does not: the script must itself handle compound commands, $( ) and backtick substitution, /usr/bin/aws, `env AWS_PROFILE=x aws ...`, `xargs aws`, and `bash -c "aws ec2 ..."`, because matcher filters by tool name only and the optional `if` filter is best-effort and fails open on commands it cannot parse. A crashed hook, or any exit code other than 2 with no JSON on stdout, drops the call back into the normal permission flow.
sheets.version_caveat: PreToolUse hooks and the allow/deny/ask permissionDecision values are generally available with no plan gate; the fourth value "defer" exists only in headless -p runs behind an Agent SDK wrapper. If you implement the guard as a prompt-type hook instead, note that from v2.1.210 a denial ends the turn by default unless you set continueOnBlock to true.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook matching Bash that parses the command and returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision "allow" only for the exact approved invocation aws s3 ls, and "deny" (or exit 2) for every other aws command. Crucially it must be the sole mechanism: no broad Bash(aws *) deny rule alongside it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A permissions rule pair, deny Bash(aws *) plus allow Bash(aws s3 ls). It loses because rules are evaluated deny first and rule specificity does not change that order, so the broad deny would also block the one call the team wants to permit; a deny rule cannot carry an allowlist exception.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs the hook before the permission prompt and honours its verdict, and a hook that exits 2 blocks the call even ahead of an allow rule; the model does not get to argue with the outcome.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs out of process with tool_input.command on stdin. Only the decision and permissionDecisionReason cross back, and asymmetrically: a deny reason is shown to Claude so it can adapt, while an allow reason is shown to the user only.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs before the permission prompt on every Bash tool call in sessions that load the hook, for the whole session. It stops applying when the settings source is removed, and it does nothing about AWS access reached through any tool other than Bash, such as an MCP server.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on hook malfunction: only exit code 2 blocks, while exit code 1 is treated as a non-blocking error and the command proceeds. Command parsing is the other weak point, since aws s3 ls && aws iam list-users, a sh -c wrapper, an env-var prefix or an absolute /usr/local/bin/aws path can slip past a naive prefix test, so the hook must default-deny anything it cannot positively classify.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on PreToolUse allow and deny decisions, and no plan restriction. The shape caveat matters instead: PreToolUse must return its verdict inside hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision, because the older top-level decision and reason fields are deprecated for this event, so a hook copied from an old example may not enforce anything.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool implementing an explicit allowlist: parse the command, and if it is a single simple command that is exactly the approved read-only invocation with no shell metacharacters, return an allow decision so it runs without prompting; if it is any other aws invocation, or anything the parser cannot fully resolve, return deny.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Expressing it purely as settings.json permission rules, an allow entry for the one command plus a deny entry covering the aws prefix. This is rejected because deny is evaluated ahead of allow, so a blanket aws deny also kills the one command that is supposed to pass, and enumerating every other aws subcommand as a deny is not exhaustive.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook decision is applied before execution and the allow path is what removes the prompt, so neither the block nor the exemption depends on the model.
sheets.context_boundary: Parsing runs out of process on the tool input string. Only the decision and a short reason cross back, which is also how the agent learns to stop trying other aws commands.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash call for the whole session, and it lapses if the hook is unregistered or if aws is reached some other way, for example through a Python boto3 script or an MCP server that wraps the same API.
sheets.failure_mode: Command-string allowlisting fails open against composition unless it is written paranoid: a semicolon or && chain, an env prefix, an absolute path to the binary, quoting tricks, aws with a profile flag, or the command passed through sh -c all evade a naive equality check. Default-deny on anything unparsed is what turns this into a fail-closed control. Conversely an over-strict matcher rejects the legitimate call with extra flags and the team routes around the hook.
sheets.version_caveat: The important semantics here are the prefix-matching grammar for Bash permission specifiers and the deny-over-allow precedence, plus the ability of a PreToolUse hook to return an allow decision that suppresses the prompt. I cannot verify the exact matcher grammar or that allow-from-hook fully bypasses prompting on the installed version from model knowledge alone, so both need a live test.
